Dry mouth (xerostomia and hyposalivation)

Some trials report improved flow or symptoms, while other sham-controlled comparisons find little or no added benefit. Outcomes vary by the cause of dryness.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Some trials report improved flow or symptoms, while other sham-controlled comparisons find little or no added benefit. Outcomes vary by the cause of dryness.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact category contains 44 records: 33 human clinical reports, nine reviews or meta-analyses, and two study protocols. Reviews summarize overlapping primary studies and are not additional cohorts. Human studies include sham-controlled trials, non-randomized comparisons and single-arm reports across cancer treatment, medication-related dryness, Sjögren syndrome and other causes. No animal or in-vitro/ex-vivo study is listed.

Human and clinical evidence

Several studies report improved flow or symptoms, including some head-and-neck radiotherapy and dialysis cohorts; other controlled results are null. A sham-controlled Sjögren trial found no improvement in symptoms or flow, and a radiotherapy RCT found no between-group difference in xerostomia or flow (Fidelix et al., 2018; Louzeiro et al., 2020). A later sham-controlled trial reported symptom/quality-of-life improvement, illustrating the mixed evidence (Ferrandez-Pujante et al., 2022). Etiology is a major source of heterogeneity: residual salivary-gland function after radiotherapy is not interchangeable with autoimmune, metabolic, dialysis-related, or medication-associated dryness. Subjective xerostomia and measured salivary flow are also distinct outcomes. The database does not support one common effect estimate across these populations, devices, wavelengths, schedules, and follow-up periods.

Primary original study: Lopez-Garzon et al. 2025

Animal evidence

none identified.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

none identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The 2025 sham-controlled radiotherapy trial used 830 nm near-infrared light at 53 mW and 7.5 J/cm² for 24 sessions, twice weekly for 3 months. The trial reported a near-significant interaction for dry-mouth symptoms and a near-significant salivary-flow result. Its regimen concerns post-radiotherapy dysfunction and is not automatically generalizable to other causes.

Interpretation

The cause of dryness matters because remaining gland function, autoimmune disease, medication exposure, and cancer treatment differ. Symptom ratings and salivary-flow tests should be read separately. The evidence does not establish a uniform effect across etiologies or show that one schedule should be used for all forms of xerostomia.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow. Salivary flow or symptoms may improve in some groups, but controlled results vary by cause.
Publications and records44 unique titles.

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The human literature spans radiotherapy, Sjögren syndrome, dialysis, medication-related dryness, and other causes. Subjective xerostomia and measured salivary flow are separate outcomes. Some controlled studies report improvement while others are null, and reviews reuse overlapping trials. A single effect estimate across these populations is not justified.
